## Background

Scientific image analysis is usually fragmented across disconnected tools: one application to annotate images, another script to prepare datasets, another framework to train a model, notebooks to evaluate it, and yet another platform to share the result. For students and non-specialists, this fragmentation also makes deep learning look like a black box.

**AnnoTrain** connects these steps into a single workflow:

> Human annotation → Dataset → Training → Evaluation → Model → Sharing → Reuse → Improvement

A researcher can create a project, share a simple annotation link, collect annotations from students, colleagues, or citizen scientists, build a quality-controlled dataset, and optionally train and evaluate a deep-learning model, inspecting its predictions, correcting its errors, and publishing the resulting dataset and model. A contributor's experience stays as simple as: **open link → annotate → next image**, no account required.

## Ambition

AnnoTrain is built around four pillars: **participatory annotation, deep learning, education, and open science**. It is not meant to replace specialized annotation tools such as CVAT or Label Studio, but to combine citizen science, scientific annotation, model training, and teaching in one accessible platform, generic enough to support classification, detection, segmentation, point/landmark annotation, and eventually tracking, across domains ranging from camera-trap ecology to plant root imaging and microscopy.

A first pedagogical prototype is being built for the *Bioinformatics Tools* MSc course at the University of Neuchâtel (session *A First Neural Network*, planned for November 2026), where students annotate camera-trap images and directly build the dataset used to train their first neural network. On the research side, [DeepPlate](DeepPlate.html) - an existing U-Net segmentation model for plate-based plant phenotyping - is a target early use case for validating human-in-the-loop model improvement inside AnnoTrain.
